title: Perforated peptic ulcer

header.contentArea: MRCS Part B • emergency surgical decision-making

related.why: surgical sepsis; both test timely source control
sigmoid volvulus; both test timely source control

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee in the emergency surgical assessment unit. A 54-year-old patient has sudden severe epigastric pain and now looks acutely unwell.
brief.task: Review the observations and imaging request and explain immediate management to the examiner. A simulated nurse answers operational questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Suspect hollow-viscus perforation and septic/hypovolaemic shock; stabilise in parallel with urgent surgical source control.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating the CT or an erect film as a prerequisite to urgently resuscitating and involving the consultant.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: I am worried about perforation with shock. Please call the consultant surgeon and anaesthetist while I start ABCDE.

flow: Recognise peritonitis and physiological shock immediately.
ABCDE, monitoring, oxygen if indicated, two IV lines, bloods/cultures as appropriate, blood gas/lactate, crossmatch, fluids guided by response and urinary catheter.
Keep nil by mouth; IV analgesia, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics according to local intra-abdominal sepsis policy, IV PPI as clinically appropriate, NG decompression according to senior assessment.
Urgent consultant and anaesthetic review; CT with IV contrast if stable enough, without delaying life-saving intervention.
Arrange urgent operative source control; anticipate deterioration, ICU, and subsequent H. pylori/NSAID risk review.

grid.label: Recognise emergency
grid.fail: Calls it indigestion and misses shock.
grid.borderline: Identifies abdominal emergency but no explicit shock assessment.
grid.pass: Identifies likely perforation, peritonitis and shock.
grid.high: Explains life-threatening sepsis/contamination and immediate parallel actions.

grid.label: ABCDE and escalation
grid.borderline: Requests help late without named teams.
grid.pass: Uses ABCDE and urgently calls consultant and anaesthesia.
grid.high: Delegates actions with explicit re-evaluation and critical care planning.

grid.label: Access and monitoring
grid.fail: No IV access or continuous observations.
grid.pass: Two IV cannulas; ECG/SpO₂/BP monitoring; repeat physiology.
grid.high: Plans invasive monitoring if indicated with anaesthesia/critical care.

grid.label: Investigations
grid.borderline: Bloods but no lactate or crossmatch.
grid.pass: FBC, U&Es, CRP, clotting, blood gas/lactate, group/crossmatch.
grid.high: Explains serial lactate and tests do not delay treatment.

grid.label: Resuscitation
grid.fail: Withholds resuscitation while waiting for CT.
grid.pass: Gives appropriate IV resuscitation and reassesses perfusion/urine output.
grid.high: Anticipates repeated assessment, overload risk, blood products or pressors with senior team.

grid.label: Contamination management
grid.borderline: Nil by mouth but delayed antimicrobials.
grid.pass: Nil by mouth, timely IV antibiotics, analgesia; consider NG/PPI under team plan.
grid.high: Explains local antibiotic choice, allergy check and source-control priority.

grid.label: Imaging decision
grid.pass: CT if safe; unstable patient requires immediate senior decision on surgery.
grid.high: Uses imaging to plan treatment but never substitutes it for source control.

grid.label: Surgery/source control
grid.pass: Urgent operative source control; discusses repair/lavage options with consultant.
grid.high: Anticipates laparoscopic/open approach based on physiology and perforation characteristics.

grid.label: Reassessment and communication
grid.borderline: Notes falling BP but no response plan.
grid.pass: Escalates new shock, repeat ABCDE and reassess fluid/organ support.
grid.high: Provides concise SBAR and explains severity and aftercare to patient/family.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. Where exactly is the pain?

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: All over now; it started very suddenly high in my abdomen.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Perhaps it is gastritis. Are you taking painkillers?

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Ibuprofen most days. I feel faint.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Nurse: His BP is 88/54 and his pulse is 124.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Let us wait for the CT result before starting fluids or calling the consultant.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The abdomen is rigid. Does that change your plan?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will arrange an abdominal film first. Antibiotics can wait until we confirm the diagnosis.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What access, monitoring and tests do you want?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: He does not need a cannula or monitoring yet; an abdominal radiograph is the only test I need.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Nurse: He is getting more drowsy and BP is now 78/46.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Perhaps he is anxious. We can repeat observations in an hour.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you still send him for CT now?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, CT must come first, whatever his blood pressure does.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is a surgical emergency. A rigid abdomen, tachycardia and BP 88/54 suggest perforation with shock. Please contact the on-call consultant surgeon and anaesthetist now.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Nurse: They are being paged. What would you like first?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will assess airway and breathing, repeat full observations, attach ECG, pulse oximetry and frequent BP, and obtain two wide-bore cannulas.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Nurse: The patient is alert but distressed. Oxygen saturation remains 95% on air.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Please take FBC, U&Es, CRP, liver tests, clotting, venous blood gas and lactate, and group and crossmatch. Record a fluid balance chart.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Lactate is 4.1 mmol/L. What do you do before imaging?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Begin careful IV crystalloid resuscitation with repeated BP and perfusion checks, give IV analgesia, keep nil by mouth, and administer IV broad-spectrum antibiotics under the local intra-abdominal sepsis policy after an allergy check. I will consider NG decompression with the senior team.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes, CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast if stable enough, but I will not delay consultant review or surgery in an unstable patient.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: CT now shows free gas and fluid near the duodenal bulb. Interpret this.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This supports perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis. They need urgent operative source control, with laparoscopy or laparotomy and repair as appropriate to physiology and operative findings.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Nurse: His blood pressure has fallen to 78/46.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Please activate emergency senior and anaesthetic support at the bedside. Repeat ABCDE and lactate, reassess fluid response, catheterise for urine-output monitoring and prepare for theatre and higher-level care.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What should happen after the operation?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Monitor for sepsis, leak and organ dysfunction; review ulcer risk, avoid NSAIDs when possible, and test/treat H. pylori according to the definitive diagnosis and senior plan.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before any further history, this is presumed upper gastrointestinal perforation with peritonitis and shock: BP 88/54, pulse 124 and a rigid abdomen. Nurse, please summon consultant surgery and anaesthesia immediately; I will lead ABCDE until they arrive.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Nurse: I have sent both calls.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Is the airway patent, what is the work of breathing, and is there ongoing vomiting? Apply continuous pulse oximetry and ECG, cycle BP frequently, and establish two large-bore peripheral IV lines.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Nurse: He is talking, breathing quickly and retching, with saturation 95%.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Oxygen only if clinically needed; suction available. Please send FBC, U&Es, liver tests, clotting, inflammatory markers, gas including lactate, and group and crossmatch; confirm drug allergies, anticoagulants and antibiotic timing.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The lactate is 4.1. What is your immediate therapeutic plan?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Keep nil by mouth, give titrated IV analgesia and prompt broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials covering intra-abdominal contamination according to local guidance, and resuscitate with crystalloid in reassessed increments. We need repeated mental state, pulse pressure, capillary refill, lactate and urine output—not fluid on autopilot.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The radiology team can obtain CT, but there is a short delay.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If he responds and transfer is safe, contrast CT defines the perforation. With continuing shock, imaging must not become a barrier to timely surgery. I would brief the consultant and anaesthetic team now to coordinate source control.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: CT shows free gas around the duodenal bulb and intraperitoneal fluid.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would present this as a likely perforated duodenal ulcer. Management is urgent operative repair with lavage, selecting laparoscopic versus open surgery based on physiology and surgical judgement; discuss gastric biopsy or alternative repair if operative findings demand it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Nurse: His BP has dropped to 78/46. He is now more drowsy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That is evolving refractory shock. Activate immediate bedside consultant/anaesthetic response, repeat ABCDE, reassess volume status and perfusion, obtain repeat gas, and prepare for vasopressor support, organ support and urgent theatre with the critical-care team.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What would you tell the family?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would explain plainly that there may be a hole in the stomach or duodenum causing infection and dangerously low blood pressure, that urgent treatment and an operation are likely, and that the team will update them as decisions are made.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Document perforation cause and treatment; arrange H. pylori assessment and eradication when indicated, NSAID review and follow-up, with operative and microbiology findings guiding duration of therapy.

failures.move: Waits for CT while patient is in shock.
Attempts prolonged non-operative observation despite diffuse peritonitis.

recovery.when: If you have been focusing on imaging
recovery.line: I have been focusing on imaging; I need to correct course—this patient is shocked. I am calling the consultant and anaesthetist while I start resuscitation.

recovery.when: If there is no CT report yet
recovery.line: Even without a CT report, a rigid abdomen and worsening physiology make source control urgent; I will escalate immediately.

knowledge.fact: Rigid peritonitis with shock requires urgent resuscitation and surgical review.
Contrast CT is recommended for diagnostic definition, provided instability does not delay emergency treatment.
Early broad-spectrum IV antibiotics cover perforation-related intra-abdominal infection.
Emergency surgery is recommended in peritonitis or clinically significant pneumoperitoneum.
Laparoscopic versus open repair depends on physiologic stability and ulcer characteristics.
Escalation and observation frequency respond to physiology and clinical concern.

recall.think: Treat as perforation with peritonitis and shock from the outset.
recall.say: “This needs senior surgical and anaesthetic action now.”
do: ABCDE, two IV lines, cultures/lactate/crossmatch, resuscitate and give IV antibiotics.

numbers.meaning: No fixed fluid volume replaces reassessment.

recall.trap: Do not postpone resuscitation or surgery just to obtain another image.
recall.finish: Theatre source control, organ support and ulcer-risk follow-up.

partner.actorBrief: Simulated patient/nurse or examiner cues: reveal only at the specified time; maintain exactly the same results in all performances. Opening: “My stomach suddenly hurt terribly and now it hurts everywhere.” Never volunteer a medication history unless asked.

reveals.finding: CT free gas and fluid near duodenal bulb.
